citation: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB (2014). The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. British journal of sports medicine.
population: Athletes and sports participants across 25 randomized controlled trials (26,610 participants, 3,464 injuries)
intervention: Exercise interventions including strength training, stretching, proprioception training, and combinations of these
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 RCTs found that exercise interventions overall reduced sports injuries, but effects varied by type. Strength training, proprioception training, and multiple-exposure programmes showed significant injury reduction, while stretching alone did not. Both acute and overuse injuries were reduced by physical activity programmes.
key_findings: Overall effect estimate on injury prevention was heterogeneous across studies.
Stretching showed no beneficial effect: RR 0.963 (95% CI 0.846-1.095).
Multiple-exposure programmes reduced injuries: RR 0.655 (95% CI 0.520-0.826).
Proprioception training reduced injuries: RR 0.550 (95% CI 0.347-0.869).
Strength training reduced injuries to less than one-third: RR 0.315 (95% CI 0.207-0.480).
Intention-to-treat sensitivity analyses yielded even more robust effect estimates.
effect_size: Overall heterogeneous; stretching RR 0.963 (0.846-1.095); multiple exposures RR 0.655 (0.520-0.826); proprioception RR 0.550 (0.347-0.869); strength training RR 0.315 (0.207-0.480); acute injuries RR 0.647 (0.502-0.836); overuse injuries RR 0.527 (0.373-0.746)
limitations: Abstract only; high heterogeneity across trials; 12 studies required adjustment for clustering effects; potential publication bias (Harbord's small-study effects) noted.
